The Catalonian barbel Barbus haasi exhibits a relatively modest ultimate total length, with field surveys documenting a maximum recorded size of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm]. This value places the species among the smaller members of the genus Barbus inhabiting Iberian river systems. Reproductive females attain a body length at puberty of 9.8 cm [Lp = 9.8 cm], a threshold that appears to be reached after approximately two growing seasons under prevailing thermal conditions. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical power-law trajectory, and from this growth pattern the wet weight at puberty has been calculated at 9.6 g [Wwp = 9.6 g], representing a substantial increase from neonatal mass. The progression from juvenile to reproductively competent female is thus accompanied by a pronounced accumulation of somatic tissue, a pattern consistent with the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning activity in cyprinids.

At the initiation of the life cycle, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0035 g [Wwb = approximately 0.0035 g], a value derived from the mean egg diameter of 1.888 mm observed in gravid females captured during the spring spawning season. This small initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva during the brief lecithotrophic phase following chorion rupture. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae remain entirely dependent on endogenous nutrients and commence first exogenous feeding only after mouth opening and yolk absorption completion, a critical trophic switch that occurs within the first week of development. The modest size of the freshly ovulated egg, with its transparent chorion and lipid droplet, is typical for a rheophilic cyprinid adapted to moderate-flow Mediterranean streams. The transition from yolk-dependent embryo to actively feeding pelagic larva is a period of high mortality, and the relatively small energy reserve at birth may constrain survival under suboptimal prey densities.

At a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) for mature females, sampled during the pre-spawning period, was 13% [GSI = 13%]. At the same experimental temperature, the maximum lifespan recorded for this species in both wild and captive populations reaches approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days], equivalent to roughly eight years of sustained physiological activity at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This longevity is notable among small-bodied Iberian barbels and implies a life-history strategy that balances relatively late maturation with extended reproductive tenure. The consistency of the thermal regime across both the reproductive index and the lifespan estimate suggests that the population experiences a relatively stable thermal environment throughout much of its active annual cycle.

The asymptotic adult body size, as defined by the ultimate wet weight, reaches approximately 282.4 g [Wwi = approximately 282.4 g] in well-provisioned individuals inhabiting productive stretches of river. This maximum mass is achieved through a growth trajectory that decelerates markedly after the onset of sexual maturation, a pattern common among cyprinids that invest heavily in gonadal tissue each reproductive season. The relationship between length and mass in this species, quantified from extensive field measurements, indicates that a female at the ultimate total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] would typically attain this peak weight, though individual variation is influenced by local food availability and intra-specific competition. Comparatively, the wet weight at puberty of 9.6 g [Wwp = 9.6 g] represents less than four percent of this ultimate mass, highlighting the extensive post-maturation growth that occurs as females continue to increase in size across multiple breeding seasons. This growth pattern is consistent with a strategy common to many temperate cyprinids, where females continue to grow substantially after reaching sexual maturity.

The total length at which females first achieve reproductive competence, 9.8 cm [Lp = 9.8 cm], represents a critical developmental threshold that is typically crossed during the second or third year of life. From a life-history perspective, achieving this size before initiating vitellogenesis ensures that sufficient abdominal capacity exists to accommodate the developing ovary and its complement of eggs. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 9.6 g [Wwp = 9.6 g] reflects the somatic condition necessary to support the energetic costs of gamete production. In populations inhabiting cooler, less productive headwater streams, the attainment of this size may be delayed by an additional growing season compared to conspecifics in warmer, more productive lower reaches. The species thus exhibits considerable phenotypic plasticity in its maturation schedule, an adaptive response to the environmental heterogeneity typical of Mediterranean lotic ecosystems. Understanding these size thresholds is essential for informing conservation strategies aimed at preserving the species' reproductive potential.
